headings.title: Definition and Normal Partographic Progress
headings.content: Prolonged labour, clinically referred to as obstructed or delayed labour, occurs when labour fails to progress at a normal rate, leading to an abnormally prolonged duration. In normal obstetrical practice, understanding the partograph is vital for tracking this progress. The partograph is a graphical representation of labour used to monitor cervical dilatation and fetal well-being. According to World Health Organization standards, the active phase of labour begins at 5 cm of cervical dilation (previously 4 cm) and should progress at a rate of at least 1 cm per hour. The partograph features two critical lines: the alert line and the action line, which is drawn four hours to the right of the alert line. When the cervicograph crosses the alert line, it serves as a warning that labour may be prolonged, requiring increased vigilance and transfer from a primary health centre to a comprehensive emergency obstetric care facility. If the plot crosses the action line, immediate management and definitive intervention are mandatory to prevent severe maternal and fetal morbidity. For Nigerian nursing students, mastering the interpretation of the partograph is an essential competency. Nurses must accurately plot cervical dilation, descent of the fetal head, and uterine contractions every four hours or more frequently if indicated. Recognizing deviations from the normal curve early prevents delayed referrals, which are a major contributor to maternal mortality in resource-constrained settings. Constant monitoring ensures that any arrest in the latent or active phase of the first stage of labour, or delay in the second stage, is identified promptly before complications escalate.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Underlying Causes of Prolonged Labour
headings.content: The pathophysiology of prolonged labour is multifaceted, commonly understood through the traditional obstetrical framework of the 'three Ps': Power, Passenger, and Passage. 'Power' refers to inadequate uterine contractions, which can be primary dysfunctional labour or secondary uterine inertia where contractions weaken and stop after a period of strong activity. 'Passenger' encompasses fetal factors such as macrosomia, abnormal presentations like brow or face, and malpositions like persistent occipitoposterior position, which prevent optimal engagement and descent through the pelvis. 'Passage' relates to abnormalities of the maternal bony pelvis, such as a contracted pelvis due to malnutrition, childhood rickets, or female genital mutilation, as well as soft tissue obstructions like uterine fibroids or full bladders. In the Nigerian context, early childhood malnutrition and adolescent pregnancy often contribute to contracted pelves, making cephalo-pelvic disproportion (CPD) a primary cause of obstructed labour. When these mechanical or functional barriers occur, the myometrium initially responds with increased frequency and intensity of contractions to overcome the resistance. However, if the obstruction persists, the uterine muscles undergo hypertonus followed by exhaustion, leading to a standstill in labour. Prolonged unmitigated pressure on maternal soft tissues impairs blood supply, causing local ischemia, necrosis, and potentially life-threatening complications such as uterine rupture or vesicovaginal fistulae (VVF). Understanding these root causes helps student nurses anticipate which patients are at high risk and prepare for urgent interventions.

headings.title: Clinical Assessment and Diagnosis in the Nigerian Context
headings.content: Clinical assessment and diagnosis of prolonged labour in Nigeria require a systematic, holistic, and prompt approach, especially given the delays often experienced in reaching tertiary health facilities. When a parturient woman presents, the nurse must conduct a thorough history focusing on the duration of labour, time of rupture of membranes, and parity. Physical examination begins with a general assessment of maternal vital signs to check for signs of exhaustion, dehydration, tachycardia, and fever, which may indicate developing intrauterine infection (chorioamnionitis). Abdominal examination is performed to assess fundal height, lie, presentation, engagement of the fetal head, and the strength, frequency, and duration of uterine contractions. Palpation of Bandl's ring—a pathological retraction ring rising between the upper and lower uterine segments—is a critical sign indicating impending uterine rupture. Vaginal examination is essential to determine the degree of cervical effacement and dilation, the status of the membranes, the presence of caput succedaneum or molding of the fetal skull bones, and the exact station and position of the presenting part. The nurse must also assess the pelvis for adequacy and check for the presence of vaginal discharge, meconium staining, or offensive smelling liquor. In the Nigerian healthcare system, nurses often act as frontline triage officers; therefore, their ability to document findings accurately on the partograph and communicate red flags to the attending obstetrician can mean the difference between a safe delivery and catastrophic maternal-fetal outcomes.

headings.title: Maternal and Fetal Complications
headings.content: Prolonged labour poses severe, life-threatening risks to both the mother and the developing fetus if not aggressively managed. Maternal complications arise from prolonged mechanical pressure, dehydration, exhaustion, and infection. Dehydration and electrolyte imbalances are common due to prolonged physical exertion and inadequate fluid intake. Maternal exhaustion can lead to postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) because the tired myometrium fails to contract effectively after delivery to clamp down on placental site blood vessels. Intrauterine infection, or chorioamnionitis, can rapidly progress to severe sepsis, septic shock, and multi-organ failure. One of the most devastating long-term consequences, particularly prevalent in settings with delayed access to emergency care like parts of Nigeria, is obstructed labour injury complex, which includes obstetric fistulae (vesicovaginal and rectovaginal fistulae) caused by pressure necrosis of the soft tissues between the fetal head and maternal pelvis. Furthermore, catastrophic acute events such as uterine rupture carry an extremely high risk of maternal mortality from hemorrhagic shock. Fetal complications are equally grave. Prolonged compression of the umbilical cord and placenta leads to acute or chronic intrauterine hypoxia, resulting in non-reassuring fetal heart patterns, meconium aspiration syndrome, low Apgar scores at birth, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE), cerebral palsy, and neonatal death. Understanding these wide-ranging complications reinforces why nursing students must prioritize timely recognition and intervention.

headings.title: Immediate Nursing Care and Supportive Management
headings.content: Immediate nursing care and supportive management are critical components of stabilizing a patient experiencing prolonged labour. Upon identifying that labour is delayed or obstructed, the nurse must immediately institute supportive measures to optimize both maternal and fetal conditions while preparing for definitive medical or surgical intervention. First, establishing intravenous access with a large-bore cannula is essential for aggressive fluid resuscitation and administration of prescribed medications. The nurse should administer intravenous crystalloids (such as normal saline or Ringer's lactate) to correct maternal dehydration and correct any electrolyte imbalances. Continuous or frequent monitoring of maternal vital signs—including temperature, pulse, blood pressure, and respiratory rate—helps detect early signs of sepsis or shock. Monitoring fetal well-being via intermittent auscultation or continuous electronic fetal monitoring is crucial to identify signs of fetal distress. Passing an indwelling urinary catheter (such as a Foley catheter) keeps the bladder empty, prevents bladder trauma during examinations, improves the descent of the fetal head if obstruction is partly due to a distended bladder, and allows accurate monitoring of urine output, which is a key indicator of renal perfusion and fluid status. Pain relief and psychological support are also vital; reassuring the exhausted, anxious mother and providing a calm environment can significantly reduce stress. The nurse must document all findings, interventions, and timing meticulously, ensuring effective handover to the medical team.

headings.title: Medical and Surgical Interventions
headings.content: Medical and surgical interventions for prolonged labour depend strictly on the underlying cause, the stage of labour, and the status of the mother and fetus. If prolonged labour is due to hypotonic uterine inertia in the first stage of labour and cephalo-pelvic disproportion (CPD) has been definitively ruled out, medical augmentation using oxytocin infusion may be indicated. Oxytocin stimulates rhythmic uterine contractions, but it must be administered cautiously using an infusion pump with continuous fetal monitoring to prevent uterine hyperstimulation, which can cause fetal distress or uterine rupture. If CPD is diagnosed, or if there are signs of severe fetal distress, thick meconium staining, chorioamnionitis, or failed augmentation, immediate surgical intervention via emergency lower segment caesarean section (LSCS) is mandatory. In the second stage of labour, if the cervix is fully dilated, the membranes are ruptured, the fetal head is deeply engaged, and the maternal pelvis is adequate, operative vaginal delivery using vacuum extraction or forceps may be performed by trained personnel to expedite delivery. However, if any doubt exists regarding pelvic capacity or the safety of instrumental delivery, LSCS remains the safest route. If uterine rupture has already occurred, emergency laparotomy is required immediately to repair or remove the uterus (hysterectomy) and control hemorrhage. Nursing students must understand these interventions to assist efficiently during theatre procedures, monitor post-operative recovery, and provide vigilant post-partum care.

headings.title: Prevention Strategies and Partograph Utilization
headings.content: Prevention strategies and correct partograph utilization are the cornerstone of reducing the incidence and morbidity of prolonged labour in Nigeria. Prevention begins at the primary healthcare level through comprehensive antenatal care (ANC), where pregnant women are educated on the signs of labour, the importance of skilled birth attendance, and the dangers of home deliveries or prolonged labor managed by unskilled traditional birth attendants. Antenatal screening helps identify risk factors early, such as short stature, previous difficult deliveries, malpresentations, or signs of nutritional deficiencies that may affect pelvic development. Furthermore, healthcare facilities must enforce the universal and correct use of the partograph for every woman in active labour. Nurses and midwives must be adequately trained and supervised to plot cervical dilation diligently and act upon the alert and action lines without hesitation. Community-level interventions, such as improving transportation networks, strengthening emergency obstetric and newborn care (EmONC) referral systems, and community sensitization programs, are equally vital to ensure that pregnant women reach appropriate facilities before labour becomes dangerously prolonged. By combining rigorous clinical monitoring, adherence to partograph guidelines, and robust community engagement, nursing professionals play a pivotal role in eliminating preventable maternal and neonatal deaths associated with prolonged and obstructed labour.
